idiom_name: base class whose private/protected primitives are inherited, with a raise-NotImplementedError entry method (ApplicationController shape)
implementation_notes: Ruby's access control is per-object, not per-class, and the official Module documentation states the difference explicitly: subclasses already have access to all methods defined in the parent class, even private ones, while protected additionally allows different objects of the same class to call the method with a receiver. So the primitive API is inherited by default - mark primitives private when they must never be called with an explicit receiver, protected when siblings may call each other's primitives - and the sandbox method is an ordinary method that raises NotImplementedError, because Ruby has no abstract keyword. Where the family should not inherit state, the primitives become a module that the behaviours include, which is the idiomatic Ruby alternative to the base class. Rails shows the everyday form: controllers subclass ApplicationController and compose actions from the provided render, redirect_to and head operations.
code_sketch:
class Superpower
  def activate = raise(NotImplementedError, 'implement activate')   # the sandbox method

  private

  def play_sound(id, volume = 1.0) = sound_engine.play(id, volume)    # primitives
  def spawn_particles(kind, count) = particles.spawn(kind, count)
end

class SkyLaunch < Superpower
  def activate                              # composes primitives only
    play_sound(SOUND_SPROING)
    spawn_particles(PARTICLE_DUST, 10)
  end
end
pitfalls: private primitives cannot be called with an explicit receiver at all (self.play_sound raises NoMethodError), so a behaviour that needs one - or a sibling that must call another instance's primitive - requires protected instead.
There is no abstract enforcement: forgetting the sandbox method fails at call time with NotImplementedError, not at load time, so a behavioural test suite is the only guard.

Monkey patching and method_missing can silently add or intercept primitives; a subclass patching the base after load changes every behaviour at once, and the resulting NoMethodError points at the wrong file.
protected dispatches without inline caching and is measurably slower than private in hot paths; use it only where cross-instance calls are genuinely needed.
